title: Short Stuff: Bedbugs
summary: Short Stuff episode on bed bugs. Josh and Chuck cover the resurgence of bed bugs after DDT was banned, especially in New York and Philadelphia, and attribute it to the ban plus increased international travel. They describe bed bugs' appearance (about a quarter inch long, flat), hiding spots, rust-colored fecal spots as a sign, and checking hotel rooms before unpacking. They explain feeding (3 to 10 minutes, possible rash, itching, swelling, no known disease transmission), that bed bugs can go a year without feeding, and that cleanliness is not a prerequisite for an infestation. Treatment options covered include heat (dryer on high, sanitize wash cycle, whole-house heat treatment), suffocation in sealed plastic bags, dust and contact insecticides (including chrysanthemum-based and pyrethroid types), and hiring professionals. They close with advice on disposing of infested furniture or rugs so others don't pick them up, and a sign-off with listener email info.

segments.title: Introduction and DDT history
segments.summary: Josh introduces the bed bug topic, a listener request. They discuss how bed bugs were nearly eradicated with DDT in the 1950s, and how the DDT ban and international travel led to their return in cities like New York and Philadelphia.

segments.title: Bed bug biology and bites
segments.summary: The hosts describe bed bugs as small flat insects that hide in beds, couches, walls and clothing. They feed on blood for three to ten minutes, causing possible itching, rash or swelling, and no known disease transmission.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Ad break before the treatment discussion.

segments.title: Checking hotel rooms
segments.summary: Advice to inspect hotel mattress seams, sheet folds and luggage racks for rust-colored fecal spots or shed shells before unpacking. The hosts note bed bugs can go a year without feeding and that cleanliness does not prevent infestation.

segments.title: Bed bug treatment options
segments.summary: Heat treatments include drying clothes on high heat or using a sanitize wash, and whole-house heat treatment by professionals. Other options are sealing items in plastic to suffocate them, insecticides including dust and contact types (chrysanthemum-based and pyrethroid), and hiring a professional.

segments.title: Disposing of infested furniture
segments.summary: Advice to make infested couches or rugs unappealing before putting them on the curb so others don't pick them up. Josh objects to putting furniture in a landfill.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck has nothing to add and Josh closes with listener email information.
